title: Towel End
medium: Linen, silk, metal wrapped thread; plain weave, embroidered

altText: The embroidered end of a linen towel from Turkey, decorated with flowers stitched in silk and metal-wrapped thread.

context: The decorated end of a towel made in Turkey in the early 19th century. It is plain-woven linen embroidered with silk and metal-wrapped thread, and the Met's record lists flowers among its imagery.

descriptions.k: This is the end of a towel from Turkey. It is made of linen and stitched with silk and shiny metal thread. Look for flowers. Where do they shine?
descriptions.g12: This is the decorated end of a towel from Turkey, made about 200 years ago. The cloth is linen. Flowers are stitched on it with silk thread and thread wrapped in metal, which can glitter. Find a flower. What colors and shapes does it have?
descriptions.g35: A towel end is the decorated part of a long towel. This one was made in Turkey in the early 1800s from linen, with silk and metal-wrapped thread embroidered into flowers. Metal thread catches light and shimmers. Look at how the flowers are arranged. Why might a maker put so much work into a towel?
descriptions.g68: This towel end from early 19th-century Turkey is plain-woven linen embroidered in silk and metal-wrapped thread, with flowers as its main motif. Embroidered towels in the Ottoman world were often displayed and gifted as well as used, though the record does not describe this one's use. Notice how the flowers sit on the linen and how metal thread adds sparkle. How might the choice of materials make an everyday cloth feel precious?
descriptions.g910: Made in Turkey in the early 19th century, this towel end shows how Ottoman-era households elevated practical cloth with embroidery. Silk and metal-wrapped thread are worked into floral forms on plain-woven linen, and the metallic thread lends the surface a glint. Embroidered towels could be displayed or exchanged as signs of skill and hospitality, although this object's specific history is not given in the record. Consider how contrast of matte linen and lustrous thread shapes the flowers' emphasis.
descriptions.g1112: This early 19th-century Turkish towel end, catalogued separately from its original length, illustrates the Ottoman tradition of lavishly embroidered household linens that moved between utility and display. Silk and metal-wrapped thread on linen produce floral imagery whose luster depends on light and viewing angle. The fragmentary state invites caution: the Met's record does not tell us what the whole towel looked like or how it was used. Interpretation should rest on visible technique and materials rather than assumptions about ceremony or symbolism.

teacherNote.context: The embroidered end of a linen towel made in Turkey in the early 19th century, worked with silk and metal-wrapped thread. The Met's record gives no maker, workshop, or use.
directions: Have students use foil strips and thread to explore how metal changes the look of embroidery.
Discuss why only the end of an object might be saved, and what questions that raises.
Compare with an embroidered cloth from another region in the archive to look for shared flower motifs.
